overview: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a continuing state, not a nation founded in the map’s 1938 snapshot. Its people endured world war, built a National Health Service, welcomed migrants while often treating them unfairly, and saw most of the empire’s colonies gain independence. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland gained different forms of devolved government. Children’s languages, classrooms, family moves and hospital visits make this history more than a list of prime ministers.

periods.title: A changed official name before the map begins
periods.summary: The UK’s formal title reflected Northern Ireland after the Irish Free State separated. The imported 1938 label is a map snapshot, not a founding event.

periods.title: Families in world war
periods.summary: War brought evacuation for some children and ration books for households. Experiences differed across regions, classes and the wider empire.

periods.title: Health service, migration and independence
periods.summary: The NHS began in 1948. Caribbean and other migrants helped build postwar Britain despite discrimination. India became independent in 1947 and more colonies followed.

periods.title: Changing medicine and changing Britain
periods.summary: Medical tools improved, including a 1971 CT scan in London. More colonies gained independence, while communities pressed for fair treatment and Northern Ireland faced decades of conflict.

periods.title: Peace agreement and devolved government
periods.summary: The Belfast/Good Friday Agreement set principles for power-sharing and identity in Northern Ireland. Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish institutions received differing powers.

periods.title: Many languages, a continuing state
periods.summary: Welsh gained official status in Wales under a 2011 measure. The UK continues with multiple languages and differing regional institutions; no imported map endpoint marks an ending.

items.text: The name “United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland” reflects changes after the Irish Free State separated. The 1938 on this map is a data snapshot. It neither founded the UK nor made every community within it share one identity.

As empire ended, countries such as India in 1947 and Ghana in 1957 gained independence through their own movements and negotiations. Their histories are not merely chapters in Britain’s story; independence changed both former colonies and the UK.

The 1998 Belfast/Good Friday Agreement followed decades of conflict in Northern Ireland. It set out power-sharing, consent on constitutional status and the right to identify as British, Irish or both. Peace required institutions and daily work, not just one signature.

Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland now have different lawmaking powers; some matters remain with Westminster. “The UK” is therefore one state with several political conversations, not four places governed identically in every detail.

During the Second World War, some children were evacuated away from targeted cities. Food rationing began in 1940 and even clothing coupons changed for children in 1942. A wartime family might have to count coupons and count the days until someone came home.

The NHS opened in 1948 with care free at the point of delivery. In 1949 it sought staff from the West Indies. Hospitals depended on the work of nurses, porters, cleaners and others, including people whose welcome outside work could be far less generous.

The Empire Windrush arrived in 1948, but it was not the first postwar Caribbean ship. Some migrants travelled ahead of their families and faced housing shortages and racism. The journey could mean a new job and a painfully long wait to live together again.

In 1971 a London hospital produced the first CT scan on a patient. That machine helped doctors see inside a body without surgery, but a single invention did not make every illness easy to diagnose or treat.

A Welsh-speaking child can encounter Welsh in school and public services. A 2011 Welsh law gave the language official status in Wales. English is not the sole written language of the UK, and a family’s home language can differ from the language on a national document.

A Welsh Government document says “rhoi statws swyddogol i’r Gymraeg yng Nghymru,” meaning “give Welsh official status in Wales.” It is a small sample of written Welsh, sourced to the government’s Welsh-language text, not a claim that all UK residents use Welsh.

Original-language examples matter because Britain’s documents and homes have never used just one voice. This Welsh line concerns modern public services; earlier cards show the English legal names used in 1707 and 1801.

The NHS, devolved institutions and the UK itself still change over time. A map that shows a 1938 start and no end should be read as an imported coverage layer, not as proof that its borders were correct in every later year.

A child may learn about this period through a ration book, a relative’s journey from the Caribbean, a Welsh school sign or a hospital scan. Each is a real part of British life, but none is everybody’s experience.

ending.text: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland continues as a state. Its borders, institutions, languages and relationships have changed, and people within it hold different national identities. The imported 1938 snapshot does not give a founding date or certify every later polygon.
